results.reference_answer: In my diagram, I show the blade at approximately 60 degrees to the foam surface, with my force vector pushing mostly downward rather than forward along the cut line. The material tore at the midpoint where the blade veered off course. I believe the excessive downward pressure caused the blade to compress the foam instead of slicing cleanly through the paper face, because when I lightened my grip on the second attempt and focused on forward motion at a shallower 30-degree angle, the blade tracked straight and cut smoothly in two passes.

results.reference_answer: In my current design, the main sculptural form is centered horizontally and vertically within the frame, creating static symmetry that violates the asymmetry principle. This weakens visual impact because the centered mass feels anchored and predictable—the viewer's eye has no dynamic movement path, resulting in a lifeless, poster-like quality rather than an engaging spatial experience. To fix this, I will shift the primary form 30% toward the left edge and allow two of its extending elements to break the top and right borders, creating continuance. This off-center placement will introduce visual tension and imply the design extends beyond the frame, transforming the border into a window rather than a containment box. I will execute this by re-cutting the base structure and repositioning it before finalizing attachment points in my next studio session.

results.reference_answer: My three verification criteria are: First, I'll check the SKU number matches exactly what's listed in the module because that guarantees the correct product variant and avoids the square-tube version. Second, I'll physically inspect that the wire comes on a round spool, not a square tube, because the round spool prevents pre-formed kinks that would compromise my straight-line work. Third, I'll verify the gauge specification because incorrect thickness will affect both structural integrity and my ability to manipulate the wire for precise shapes—thicker gauge means more strength but harder bending, while thinner gauge offers flexibility but risks structural failure under tension.
